title: What a hadith is
hook: a report of what the Prophet ﷺ said, did, or approved

segments.voice: Yesterday: the weakest pillar, and one small, regular step to strengthen it.

Someone once asked Aisha a plain, domestic question: what did the Prophet do at home? Not in the mosque, not on the battlefield. At home. Her answer is preserved in Sahih al-Bukhari. He was busy serving his family, she said, and when the time for prayer came, he went out to pray. That small answer has been carried, person to person and then book to book, so it can be heard today. A new block begins with that kind of report: what it is, how it travels, how it's tested. Today, the hadith.
screen: `WHAT DID HE DO AT HOME?` → `AISHA ANSWERS.` → `A REPORT, CARRIED.`

segments.voice: The Arabic word hadith is usually put into English as a report, or news. In Islamic scholarship it names a report about the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and scholars sort those reports by what they carry. First, what he said. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet says the Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand other Muslims are safe. One sentence, a whole ethic, in his own words as remembered. Second, what he did. That's Aisha's answer: no command at all, only a description. People watched how he lived, so a deed reported becomes a teaching. Third, what he approved, the easiest one to miss. Also in Bukhari: a companion who led prayers kept ending his recitation with one short surah, al-Ikhlas. When the people came back, they mentioned it to the Prophet. He didn't say yes or no. He said: ask him why. The man said it describes the Most Merciful, and he loved to recite it. And the Prophet said: tell him that Allah loves him. The approval is the teaching. His silence, or his yes, to something done in front of him is reported too. Fourth, who gathers them. Sunni scholars collect reports of the Prophet carried through his companions. Shia scholars also gather reports of the Prophet, and beside them the sayings of the Imams of his family, weighed through their own collections and methods. Both treat a report about him as a serious thing to carry. So when a sentence starts with "the Prophet said", ask: said, did, or approved? And who carried it here?
screen: `WHAT HE SAID.` · `WHAT HE DID.` · `WHAT HE APPROVED.` · `WHO GATHERS THE REPORTS.`

segments.voice: Take today's hadith slowly: the Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand others are safe. Walk through yesterday with it, the moment your tongue wasn't safe for someone, a sharp text, a joke at someone's expense, and the moment your hands were a shelter, carrying, fixing, holding a door. Don't grade yourself; just notice both. If you pray, you can ask for a safe tongue; if not, rest with the sentence.
Hadith. A report of what the Prophet said, did, or approved, carried by the people who saw and heard him. Today's word.
Your line: a report. Said, did, or approved, and carried by someone. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims read hadith in collections such as Sahih al-Bukhari, hear them quoted in Friday sermons and study circles, and Sunni and Shia scholars each gather and weigh reports through their own collections.

chat.says: So is a hadith just something the Prophet said?
options: Not only. It reports what he said, what he did, or what he approved.
No, it's a short verse of the Qur'an, recited in the daily prayer.
No, it's a ruling a judge gives in court, drawn from the Qur'an.
chat.meaning: Scholars sort hadith by what they carry: what the Prophet said, what he did, and what he approved, even by his silence.

hadith.meaning: a report of what the Prophet said, did or approved

Aisha.meaning: the Prophet's wife, who told what he did at home

al-Ikhlas.meaning: a short surah that describes the Most Merciful

Imams.meaning: guides from the Prophet's family, whose sayings Shia scholars gather

notes: Bukhari 676, 10 and 7375: confirm numbers and paraphrases. In 7375 the man recited al-Ikhlas at the end of each recitation in prayer; 'every time' is a simplification.
Definition of hadith as said, did, approved (qawl, fi'l, taqrir) follows the index line; some definitions add the Prophet's descriptions. Confirm wording.
Gloss of the Arabic 'hadith' as report, speech, news: confirm against a standard lexicon.
Shia description (reports of the Prophet and the sayings of the Imams, weighed through their own collections): confirm it is fair and framed without ranking.
